## 1. Define the Research Question

**State what you will predict, and from** **what. Identify the problem the**
**model is meant to solve. Explain why the problem matters, how a**
**prediction would help, and who would use it. State whether your target**
**is continuous or dichotomous, and thus whether you use linear or**
**logistic regression.**

This project will be predicting moderate-to-severe PHQ-8 depression from
routine demographic/health variables. The question of whether or not a
person will have moderate-to-severe PHQ-8 depression ("yes"/"no") is a
dichotomous target, so we will be using logistic regression.

### Codebook

| Variable | What it measures | How it is stored in the file |
|---|---|---|
| `PHQCAT_A` | **Target.** Depressive symptom severity (PHQ-8), derived by NCHS from the eight PHQ-8 items | 1 = none/minimal, 2 = mild, 3 = moderate, 4 = severe; 8 = not ascertained (missing) |
| `AGEP_A` | Age in years (top-coded) | Number; 18–84 = years, 85 = 85+; 97 = refused, 98 = not ascertained, 99 = don't know |
| `SEX_A` | Sex | 1 = male, 2 = female; 7 = refused, 8 = not ascertained, 9 = don't know |
| `EDUCP_A` | Educational attainment | 01 = grade 0–11, 02 = 12th no diploma, 03 = GED, 04 = HS graduate, 05 = some college, 06 = associate (occ/tech), 07 = associate (academic), 08 = bachelor's, 09 = master's, 10 = professional/doctoral; 97 = refused, 98 = not ascertained, 99 = don't know |
| `RATCAT_A` | Family income-to-poverty ratio (imputed) | 01–14, from 01 = 0.00–0.49 up to 14 = 5.00 or greater; 98 = not ascertained (0 cases) |
| `MARSTAT_A` | Marital status | 1 = married/spouse present, 2 = married/spouse absent, 3 = married/spouse presence unknown, 4 = widowed, 5 = divorced, 6 = separated, 7 = never married, 8 = living with a partner; 9 = unknown (missing) |
| `BMICAT_A` | BMI category | 1 = underweight, 2 = healthy weight, 3 = overweight, 4 = obese; 9 = unknown (missing) |
| `SMKCIGST_A` | Cigarette smoking status | 1 = current every-day, 2 = current some-day, 3 = former, 4 = never, 5 = smoker/status unknown (1 case); 9 = unknown if ever smoked (missing) |
| `DISAB3_A` | Disability status (Washington Group short set) | 1 = yes, 2 = no; 9 = don't know (0 cases) |
| `PHSTAT_A` | Self-rated general health | 1 = excellent, 2 = very good, 3 = good, 4 = fair, 5 = poor; 7 = refused, 8 = not ascertained, 9 =

### Fixing the Dichotomous Target

Here I recode missingness and collapse to two classes.

```{r}

# 8 = not ascertained -> NA
dat$PHQCAT_A[dat$PHQCAT_A %in% c(8)] <- NA

# collapse to two classes; NA target stays NA (dropped later in Part 4)
dat$dep_modplus <- factor(
  dplyr::case_when(
    dat$PHQCAT_A %in% c(3, 4) ~ "mod_plus",
    dat$PHQCAT_A %in% c(1, 2) ~ "none_mild",
    TRUE                      ~ NA_character_
  ),
  levels = c("none_mild", "mod_plus")
)

table(dat$dep_modplus, useNA = "always")

dat$PHQCAT_A <- NULL # Drop the original PHQCAT_A to avoid data leakage

```


```{r}
str(dat)
```

### Imputation

**Impute the remaining missing predictors inside your recipe, and justify**
**the method you chose. (Options: `step_impute_median()` with**
**`step_impute_mode()`; `step_impute_knn()`; `step_impute_bag()`.)**

```{r}
sum(is.na(dat$PHQCAT_A))
```

Keep only the rows where `dep_modplus` is not missing. `is.na()` is `TRUE`
for missing values, and `!` flips `TRUE` to `FALSE`.

```{r}
nrow(dat)

dat <- dat[!is.na(dat$dep_modplus), ]

nrow(dat)

round(colMeans(is.na(dat)) * 100, 2)   # % missing: target + each predictor
```

**Why is it a bad idea to impute the target?**
We do not impute the target because a participant with no outcome cannot teach the
model anything, so those rows are dropped.

Now compare with listwise deletion, which would drop every student
missing anything:

```{r}
sum(complete.cases(dat))
```

Listwise deletion would keep only `r sum(complete.cases(dat))` of the
`r nrow(dat)` responses Instead, the recipe in Part 6 fills in the
missing predictors, so we keep all of them.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = dep_modplus)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

```

## 4. Build the Modeling Pipeline

**The recipe does four jobs, in this order:**

1.  **Fill missing numeric predictors with the median.**
2.  **Fill missing categorical predictors with the most common category.**
3.  **Dummy code the factors.**
4.  **Drop any column with zero variance, then center and scale**
    **everything.**

**Fill in the data argument and the selectors. The choices are**
**`all_numeric_predictors()` and `all_nominal_predictors()`.**

**Split the data into training and test sets with**
**`rsample::initial_split()`, stratified on the target. Set a seed so the**
**split can be reproduced, and state the proportions you used.**

```{r}
set.seed(559)

split    <- initial_split(dat, prop = 0.5, strata = "dep_modplus")
train_df <- training(split)
test_df  <- testing(split)

c(train = nrow(train_df), test = nrow(test_df))
```

**Write a preprocessing recipe with the recipes package. At minimum, it**
**should:**

- **Impute missing predictors**

- **Dummy code factors**

- **Remove zero variance predictors**

- **Center and scale numeric predictors**

- **Other options: lump rare categories with `step_other()` or**
  **transforming skewed predictors**
  
```{r}
# In recipes, "nominal" means factor (text columns count too), so
# all_nominal_predictors() selects the factors you made in Part 2
blueprint <- recipe(dep_modplus ~ ., data = train_df) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

blueprint
```

**Pass the recipe to `caret::train()` rather than preprocessing the data**
**yourself, so every step is learned within each cross-validation fold.**

`train()` will prep the recipe inside each fold for us. Here we prep and
bake it once, only to check the result.

```{r}
baked <- bake(prep(blueprint), new_data = NULL)
dim(baked)
sum(is.na(baked))

```

There are no missing values left, and there are more columns than we
started with, because dummy coding turned each factor into several
indicator columns.

## 5. Fit and Compare Models


### A Lambda Grid for This Data

```{r}
x_baked <- as.matrix(baked[, names(baked) != "dep_modplus"])

lambda_max <- max(glmnet(x_baked, baked$dep_modplus,
                         family = "binomial", alpha = 1)$lambda)

lambda_grid <- 10^seq(log10(lambda_max) - 4, log10(lambda_max) + 1,
                      length.out = 100)

range(lambda_grid)
```

**Use k-fold cross validation with `trainControl()`, and state the number**
**of folds.**

**Note any data leakage you are concerned about and what you did about it.**

**Fit a baseline model with `method = "null"`. It shows how well you can**
**predict without using any predictors, and it is what we will compare**
**every other model to.**

**Use half the responses for training and half for testing, as in the**
**lecture.**

`strata = "dep_modplus"` stratifies the split: it keeps the target's
distribution about the same in the training and test sets. For a
dichotomous target like this one, `initial_split()` groups the target
into two sections. Both sets had the same split of none_mild to mod_plus.

Always stratify when your outcome is
unbalanced, for example when only 10% of people are in one group.
Otherwise the test set can end up with too few people in the smaller
group to evaluate the model.

Everything in Parts 2 to 4 happened before the split, and that is fine.
None of those steps learned anything from the data: `-99` means missing
no matter who the student is. Imputation is different. It computes
medians and modes from the data, so it belongs in the recipe, where it
is learned from training data only.

The recipe takes the place of the formula `dep_modplus ~ .` in `train()`.
It also does the centering and scaling, so we no longer need `preProc`.

```{r}
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, classProbs = TRUE, summaryFunction = mnLogLoss) # returns logLoss, Accuracy, Kappa, etc.
set.seed(559)
fit_null <- train(
  blueprint,
  data = train_df,
  method = "null", metric = "logLoss", trControl = ctrl)

```
**One of the three must be the unpenalized regression, linear or logistic.**
**At least one must be regularized: lasso, ridge, or elastic net, with a**
**grid of lambda values (and alpha values for elastic net) tuned by cross**
**validation. The others can use other regularization methods or different**
**sets of predictors.**

1. Ordinary logistic regression.
*If your target is dichotomous, you are fitting logistic regression, and*
*several settings change from the linear case. Before you fit your*
*models, review the Loose Ends: Binary Outcome slide at the end of the*
*Regularization lecture, which lists what needs to change.*

```{r}
set.seed(559)
fit_glm <- train(
  blueprint,
  data = train_df,
  method = "glm", metric = "logLoss",
  trControl = ctrl)
```

### Additional models: Lasso, Ridge, and Elastic Net

**Compare at least three models in addition to the baseline. All of them**
**must use the same target and the same training data.**

### A Quick Reference

All three models minimize the same thing:

$$\text{Loss} = \text{MSE}_{\text{train}} + \lambda \times \text{Penalty}$$

- `lambda` ($\lambda$) sets how much the penalty counts. Cross
  validation chooses it from the grid built in Part 6.
- `alpha` ($\alpha$) sets which penalty is used.

| Model | `alpha` | Penalty | What it does |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Lasso | 1 | $\sum_{j=1}^{p} \lvert\beta_j\rvert$ | Can shrink a coefficient to exactly zero, which drops that predictor |
| Ridge | 0 | $\sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2$ | Shrinks every coefficient, but never to exactly zero |
| Elastic net | Between 0 and 1 | $\alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} \lvert\beta_j\rvert + \frac{1 - \alpha}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2$ | A mix of the two, useful when predictors are highly correlated |

### Lasso

Set `alpha` for the lasso, and fill in the method and the grid.

```{r}
lasso_grid <- expand.grid(
  alpha  = 1,
  lambda = lambda_grid )

set.seed(559)
fit_lasso <- train(
  blueprint,
  data = train_df,
  method = "glmnet",
  family = "binomial", metric = "logLoss",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = lasso_grid)

fit_lasso$bestTune
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(fit_lasso) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

### Ridge

Set `alpha` for ridge.

```{r}
ridge_grid <- expand.grid(
  alpha  = 0,
  lambda = lambda_grid )

set.seed(559)
fit_ridge <- train(
  blueprint,
  data = train_df,
  method = "glmnet",
  family = "binomial",
  metric = "logLoss",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = ridge_grid )

fit_ridge$bestTune
```

### Elastic Net

Let `alpha` run from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1.

```{r}
en_grid <- expand.grid(
  alpha  = seq(from = 0, to = 1, by = 0.1),
  lambda = lambda_grid)

set.seed(559)
fit_en <- train(
  blueprint,
  data = train_df,
  method = "glmnet",
  family = "binomial", 
  metric = "logLoss",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = en_grid)

fit_en$bestTune
```

### Comparing the Models

Every model was fit after `set.seed(559)`, so they all used the same 10
folds. This table puts their cross validated performance side by side.
It is the table to use when choosing a final model, before the test set
is touched.
**Use performance measures that fit your target. For a continuous target,**
**report RMSE, R2, and MAE. For a dichotomous target, report accuracy,**
**sensitivity, and specificity.**

**Include a table summarizing the cross validated performance of every**
**model.**

### CV Accuracy Table

```{r}
cv_table <- rbind(
  baseline    = getTrainPerf(fit_null),
  logistic    = getTrainPerf(fit_glm),
  lasso       = getTrainPerf(fit_lasso),
  ridge       = getTrainPerf(fit_ridge),
  elastic_net = getTrainPerf(fit_en)
)

round(cv_table[, "TrainlogLoss", drop = FALSE], 3)

cv_table[c("lasso","elastic_net"), "TrainlogLoss"]
```

**Choose a final model and justify the choice using the cross validation**
**results.**
The final model I chose is the lasso  model. I chose this model because although all models had relatively similar logLoss, the two best models (lasso and elastic net) were tied (both with a logLoss ~0.203)), and lasso is a much simpler model. Note: These differences are
marginal, and all the models are pretty weak.

### Evaluating the Final Model on The Test Set

**Evaluate the final model on the test set, once. Report its test set**
**performance. For a lasso or elastic net, report how many predictors it**
**kept. You do not need to list the coefficients; the variable importance**
**plot below shows which predictors matter.**

**Show which predictors matter most with `caret::varImp()`. The `vip`**
**package used in lecture is no longer on CRAN.**

In Project 1, choose your final model from the
cross validation table in Part 8, and evaluate only that model on the
test set.

```{r}
fit_final <- fit_lasso   # chosen from cv_table: lowest TrainlogLoss and simplest model


pred_final <- predict(fit_final, newdata = test_df)

cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_final, test_df$dep_modplus, positive = "mod_plus")
cm

library(ggplot2)

cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm$table)   # columns: Prediction, Reference, Freq

ggplot(cm_df, aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Actual", y = "Predicted", fill = "Count",
       title = "Confusion matrix: final lasso model (test set)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

**How many columns did the lasso keep, out of all the predictor columns it**
**could use after dummy coding?**

```{r}
# columns the lasso kept
sum(coef(fit_lasso$finalModel, s = fit_lasso$bestTune$lambda)[-1] != 0)

# columns it could use: everything in the baked data except symptoms
ncol(baked) - 1
```

These are the coefficients the lasso kept. The recipe centered and
scaled every predictor column, including the dummy columns, so the
coefficients are on a standardized scale. Compare their sizes, but do
not read them in raw units.

```{r}
lasso_coefs <- as.matrix(coef(fit_lasso$finalModel, s = fit_lasso$bestTune$lambda))

round(lasso_coefs[lasso_coefs[, 1] != 0, , drop = FALSE], 3)
```

```{r, fig.height = 4.6}
# varImp() comes with caret. It ranks predictors by the size of their
# standardized coefficients, scaled so the largest is 100, like vip() in lecture.
ggplot(varImp(fit_final), top = 15) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

### Part 10: Wrapping Up

Answer each question in a sentence or two.

1.  Which model had the highest performance (lowest CV log loss)? How many predictor columns did
    it keep?

    The lasso had the lowest cross-validated log loss and was the final model; it kept 21 of 22 predictor columns.

2.  Which predictors came out on top in the importance plot? Do they
    make sense?

    Self-rated health and age were the top predictors, followed by disability and never-smoker status; yes, these align with the depression literature.

3.  Listwise deletion would have kept only `r sum(complete.cases(dat))`
    of the `r nrow(dat)` responses Give one reason imputing inside the
    recipe is better than dropping those rows.

    Imputing helps us preserve the amount of data we have available for
    our work.
